actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species ranges from southern Morocco, Western Sahara and Mauritania in northwestern Africa, through northern Africa (with a southern range limit in Sudan - Wagner and Wilms 2010) and the Sahara Desert to southwestern Israel (McDiarmid et al. 1999, Egan 2007). it is widespread in the Saharan region as far south as the edge of the Sahel, with records from West Africa from Mauritania, northern Mali and Niger (Trape and Mané 2006). Records also exist for Algeria and Libya (Trape and Mané 2006). On the Arabian Peninsula, it has been reported from Tihama (the coastal area of western Yemen and extreme southwestern Saudi Arabia), where it is represented by the endemic subspecies Cerastes cerastes hoofieni (Werner et al. 1991). Unconfirmed reports from Jordan might refer to C. gasperetti. It can be found sea level up to 1,500 m asl.
documentation.population: It is a common and widespread species, and can be locally abundant in certain areas (e.g., the shores of Lake Nasser, Egypt). In Yemen, only two recent records are known from Hodeida (S. Busais pers. comm. February 2012), with a video record from Aden that is likely to represent this species (M.M. al Jamaily pers. comm. February 2012)
documentation.habitats: This viper is found in most desert habitat types with some rock formations, but not in large dune formations (Trape and Mané 2006). In Arabia animals are found in sandy patches from scrubland to low-altitude rocky barrens and foothills (Egan 2007). The species can tolerate extreme hyperarid habitats. In Africa it generally avoids the Atlantic coastal area. This crepuscular viper spends the day in burrows or beneath scree (Trape and Mané 2006). It feeds on reptiles, birds, rodents and large insects (Trape and Mané 2006). In West Africa, animals do not feed between December and February and leaves its shelter only to bask (Trape and Mané 2006). The female lays a clutch of between 10 and 20 eggs. Maximum size is 80 cm.
documentation.threats: There appear to be no major threats to this widespread species.  Animals are locally collected for exhibition by snake charmers. Large numbers are collected in Egypt and Saudi Arabia for venom extraction, and these animals are generally not released. There is no other use of this species in Arabia, although in common with other snakes it is persecuted when encountered.
documentation.measures: Its range includes several protected areas. There is a need to research the sustainability of harvests for venom extraction in parts of its range. The subspecies Cerastes cerastes hoofieni from Arabia requires genetic study to better determine its taxonomic status.
documentation.use_trade: There is localized use of this species by snake-charmers, and for venom extraction. Small numbers have been reported in the international pet trade: Jensen et al. (2019) recorded 49 animals advertised for export from Egypt and Morocco between 2013 and 2017.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, and because it is subject to no major threats.
